builds.title: Gemma 4 31B at FP8, 256K context
builds.subtitle: One 96 GB card locally, one H100 in the cloud. The model every FlatClaw tenant runs today.

model.name: Gemma 4 31B-IT
model.engine: SGLang, --quantization fp8 --tp 1, tool-call and reasoning parsers gemma4

variants.title: The one-card inference workstation
variants.summary: One 96 GB card holds Gemma 4 31B at FP8 with the full 256K window, exactly as the hosted tenant runs it; the rest of the box is an ordinary high-end desktop platform. Every part is sold by Newegg today at the price shown.

parts.pick: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q, 96 GB
parts.why: 96 GB of GDDR7 holds the 31B at FP8 with the full 256K window on one card, exactly how the hosted tenant runs it. 300 W, a quiet blower, display outputs. The 600 W Workstation Edition is a few percent faster when Newegg has it in stock; today it does not. The passive Server Edition is wrong for a tower.
Feeds the card over PCIe 5.0 and runs the OS, SGLang, the gateway and ingestion. Twelve cores is plenty; the 9950X only pays off for CPU-heavy ingestion.
Two PCIe 5.0 x16 slots (x8/x8) so a second card can follow later, 10 GbE + 2.5 GbE, four M.2, USB4: workstation-grade AM5.

parts.pick: Corsair Vengeance 64 GB (2 × 32 GB) DDR5-6000 CL30
parts.why: Two DIMMs keep AM5 at full speed; 64 GB carries the OS, Docker, the gateway and ingestion with headroom, because the model lives in VRAM. DDR5 has roughly quadrupled in price this year; 96 GB kits are not worth it for this box.
A native 12V-2×6 lead for the Pro 6000 and wide margin over the ~500 W peak of card plus platform; the same unit carries the 600 W Workstation Edition if you swap in later.

parts.pick: Corsair Nautilus II 360 RS, 360 mm AIO
parts.why: Holds the 120 W 9900X while the GPU dumps heat into the case; fits the North XL's top mount.

parts.pick: Fractal Design North XL, Mesh, charcoal and walnut
parts.why: A tower that looks like furniture: 413 mm of GPU room, a 360 mm top radiator, a mesh side feeding the blower. Mesh, not glass.
OS plus the model library (~1 TB system, ~3 TB weights); the board takes Gen5 natively.

notes: Peak draw is the card's 300 W plus about 200 W of platform: ~500 W, about 4 A at 120 V on an ordinary circuit. Quiet enough for a desk.

Ubuntu 24.04 Server with NVIDIA R570+ / CUDA 12.8+ (sm_120). The card has display outputs for a monitor when you want one and runs headless otherwise. Serve from containers and hold driver updates before demo days.
One SGLang process on the one card behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, the same launch line as the hosted tenant. The model never reloads.
Run the OpenClaw gateway and the Portal on the same box for a fully local setup, or point a separate control machine at its endpoint; both work.

software.label: Serve

cloud.lead: The same checkpoint in a tenancy on the cloud the customer already runs: Azure, AWS, Google Cloud, or our reference lane.
cloud.priceBasis: Indicative list prices held warm 24/7 on our reference lane; the same classes on Azure, AWS and Google Cloud land in the same band on reserved terms, and bare metal amortizes lower.

options.name: GPU node
options.spec: 1 × H100 80 GB · 26 vCPU · 234 GB RAM on the reference plan
notes: About $2,000 a month held warm 24/7 including the bundled CPU and RAM.
Weights are fetched from the weights volume over the tenancy's own network at boot; nothing leaves the tenancy.

options.name: Control plane
options.spec: 4 vCPU · 16 GB · the Portal plus one OpenClaw gateway per user
notes: Two or three users at 0.6–1.2 GB each with room to spare. Every tenant has this service next to its GPU, on any cloud's small VM or container plan.

options.name: Weights volume
options.spec: 200 GB of storage plus a small CPU pod that serves it over HTTP
notes: Staged once; the GPU node fetches the weights at boot because GPU plans rarely mount a volume directly.
Flat per-tenant rate, not per-token metering: the GPU line dominates and everything else is under $200.
Capacity is peak concurrent sessions, not head count: one H100 sustains 8–12 concurrent streaming chats at FP8 with first tokens in 1–2 s.
cloud.allInNote: About $2,200 a month per tenant held warm: the GPU node, the control plane and the weights volume, on whichever cloud the customer already runs.

builds.title: GLM-5.2 at FP8 on eight 96 GB cards, or eight B200s in the cloud
builds.subtitle: Only about 40B parameters are active per token, so the weights have to be held, not computed. The FP8 checkpoint is 744 GB: eight 96 GB cards in a 4U server locally, eight B200s in the cloud. A two-card workstation runs a 4-bit copy.

model.engine: SGLang at FP8 across eight cards, locally or in the cloud; llama.cpp or KTransformers for the two-card 4-bit workstation

variants.title: The FP8 server: eight cards in 4U (chosen)
variants.summary: Eight 96 GB Blackwell cards in a 4U chassis hold the 744 GB FP8 checkpoint in VRAM, the same way the cloud node does and with the same launch line. Six cards (576 GB) cannot hold it; eight is the minimum, and the remaining ~24 GB carries an FP8 KV cache for a handful of long conversations at a time. Every part is sold by Newegg today.

parts.why: Eight double-width GPU bays with the airflow and redundant 3 kW supplies to match; board, backplane and power are included. In stock at Newegg; the E12 generation is not.
Two sockets for 24 memory channels and 256 PCIe 5.0 lanes feeding eight x16 cards; the GPUs do the work. The 48- and 64-core parts are out of stock and unnecessary here.

parts.pick: Kingston Server Premier 64 GB DDR5-5600 ECC RDIMM × 12 = 768 GB
parts.why: 768 GB matches the VRAM, so the whole checkpoint can stage through system memory; one DIMM on six of the twelve channels per socket. Memory is where the money went this year.

parts.pick: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q, 96 GB
parts.why: 8 × 96 GB = 768 GB, FP8 weights in VRAM. The 300 W blower was made for dense boxes; the passive Server Edition is on Newegg only through a marketplace seller at $30,000, so the Max-Q it is.
The FP8 checkpoint alone is 744 GB; four drives hold it plus two quant tiers and the BF16 shards for conversion.

notes: 8 × 300 W plus two 280 W CPUs and the platform: about 3.2 kW, a dedicated 240 V circuit and a room that can shed the heat.

Same shape as the cloud node, which is the point: the launch line is identical, only the owner changes. Per-stream speed follows memory bandwidth, GDDR7 at 1.8 TB/s per card against the B200's 8 TB/s, so the cloud node decodes faster; this box is FP8 parity you own.
Six cards (576 GB) cannot hold the FP8 checkpoint at all, and eight leave about 24 GB for KV. For FP8 at full concurrency and the 1M window, the cloud node's 1,536 GB is the shape.

variants.title: The two-card 4-bit workstation (the cheaper path)
variants.summary: Two Blackwell cards hold attention, the shared layers and the KV cache at CUDA speed; 512 GB of 8-channel DDR5 holds the cold experts of a 4-bit copy. Decode lands around 10–18 tokens per second, prefill is CUDA-fast. Every part is on Newegg today.

parts.pick: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q, 96 GB
parts.why: Attention, dense layers, the FP8 KV cache and as many hot expert tensors as fit, split across both cards. Two Max-Q blowers at 300 W each sit side by side and run off a 1,600 W supply; the 600 W Workstation Edition pair would want 2,000 W and more airflow.
Eight DDR5 channels (~325 GB/s) feed the experts, which is the real bottleneck, plus 128 PCIe 5.0 lanes for two x16 cards and the offload engine.
sTR5 / WRX90: seven PCIe 5.0 x16 slots, eight DDR5 RDIMM slots, 10 GbE. The only desktop platform with both the lanes and the memory channels.

parts.pick: Kingston Server Premier 64 GB DDR5-5600 ECC RDIMM × 8 = 512 GB
parts.why: Holds the whole 4-bit GGUF (≈475 GB) in RAM; experts stream to the GPUs per token. All eight channels populated: bandwidth sets decode speed. Memory prices roughly quadrupled since the June 2026 sheet; this line is where the money went.
2 × 300 W Max-Q + 350 W CPU + platform ≈ 1.25 kW continuous. Native 12V-2x6 cables for both cards.
Full sTR5 cold-plate coverage for the 350 W Threadripper while two GPUs dump heat into the case.
Mesh airflow and room for two long cards and an E-ATX / SSI-EEB board. Alternative: a 4U rack chassis if it lives in a closet.
GGUF tiers run 223–810 GB each. Two 4 TB Gen5 drives hold several quant levels side by side (the 8 TB model is not listed).

notes: The engine keeps attention and KV on the cards and routes cold experts to RAM: llama.cpp (-ngl 99 -n-cpu-moe 999 -ts 50,50 --flash-attn --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0) or KTransformers for more expert throughput. OpenClaw points at the single OpenAI endpoint, exactly like the 31B box.
A 744B MoE owns all the memory: no room for image or voice on this box; run modality on a second machine as the flagship build does.
This is the cheaper path: a quantized GLM-5.2 (4-bit is excellent) at workstation speed. FP8 parity you own is the eight-card server above.

cloud.lead: The same checkpoint in a tenancy on the cloud the customer already runs. The fast node and the economy node are both eight-GPU machines; the control plane is twice the flagship tenant's.

options.name: GPU node, fast
notes: HBM3e at about 8 TB/s per card, roughly twice the H200, so decode per stream is about twice as fast; FP8 weights and an FP8 KV cache with room for the full 1M-token window.
SGLang --tp 8 --enable-moe-ep; a 1.5 TB or larger weights volume, fetched by the node at boot (744 GB).

notes: The same checkpoint and launch line at about half the decode speed; context up to 256K with KV room.

options.name: Control plane
options.spec: 8 vCPU · 32 GB · the Portal, one OpenClaw gateway per user and the failover router
notes: Twice the flagship tenant's control plane: the frontier class carries more users and longer sessions, and the router that fails over between the fast node, the economy node and a quantized fallback runs here too. Room for eight to ten users at 1–1.2 GB each.

options.spec: 1.5 TB or larger, plus a small CPU pod that serves it
notes: The GPU node fetches the checkpoint at boot; an Ampere node (A100) has no FP8 and would need a quantized copy.
Cost reality: this is a different tier. The B200 node is about seventeen times the 31B tenant held warm, so the frontier class is scheduled for live load and scaled to zero between sessions.
Per GPU-hour at reference list prices: H100 $2.74 · RTX PRO 6000 96 GB $3.00 · H200 ~$3.14 · B200 ~$5.87.
Routing is unchanged: OpenClaw points at one endpoint; a LiteLLM or vLLM router in the same tenancy adds failover to the economy node, a quantized fallback or a second region.

recipes.title: Gemma 4 31B at FP8 on one H100, 256K context
recipes.summary: What every FlatClaw tenant runs today, in a tenancy on the customer's own cloud: a public SGLang image with no weights baked in, a weights volume served over the tenancy's own network, and the Portal and one OpenClaw gateway per user on a small CPU service next to the GPU.

specs.v: 1 × H100 80 GB · about $2,000 a month held warm · Azure `NC H100 v5` · AWS `p5` · Google Cloud `A3` · reference lane `nf-gpu-h100-80-1g` (26 vCPU, 234 GB RAM bundled)
4 vCPU · 16 GB · about $144 a month · the Portal plus one gateway per user at 0.6–1.2 GB each · Azure `D4s v5` · AWS `m6i.xlarge` · Google Cloud `n2-standard-4` · reference lane `nf-compute-400-16`
`ghcr.io/skytruax/flatclaw-inference` · SGLang base plus entrypoint · about 18 GB · no weights inside
Gemma 4 31B FP8 on a 200 GB tenancy volume · staged once from Kaggle · a CPU pod serves them to the GPU pod over HTTP
Image pull, weights fetch from the tenancy's own volume, model load; the gateways come up after the control container, with the seeded users' prompts re-synced on every boot
8–12 concurrent streaming chats · first token in 1–2 seconds · the RadixAttention prefix cache carries conversational reuse

recipes.launch:
# inference pod, after the weights fetch
python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path /weights/gemma-4-31b-it --quantization fp8 --tp 1 --context-length 262144 --tool-call-parser gemma4 --reasoning-parser gemma4 --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 1 --port 8000

sections.title: How it is wired on the reference lane
items: GPU plans bundle CPU, RAM and GPU. A GPU attached to a CPU plan is silently dropped.
Managed GPU services cannot mount the read-write-once volume, so a CPU pod serves it and the GPU pod fetches the weights at boot.
Override the image's entrypoint with `customEntrypoint`, not `customCommand`, and ship multi-line scripts base64-encoded.
GPU nodes need 500 GB of ephemeral storage declared, or the deployment is refused.
Inference is a Portal setting pushed to every gateway, not a platform secret and a redeploy. A gateway's environment carries none of the Portal's secrets.

sections.title: What cost us time
items: Hopper or Blackwell for FP8. On A100-class Ampere the Marlin FP8 kernel rejects Gemma 4 31B's 8,608-wide projection, and no flag disables it.
Scale-to-zero in production: GPU scheduling queues stretch from minutes to a day. A warm GPU is the floor of the unit economics.
A moving `sglang:dev` tag split one flag into two overnight and put the pod in a restart loop while it billed. Pin what you depend on.
A redeploy restarts every gateway and aborts live runs. Treat a demo as a config freeze, and abort a superseded build rather than let two roll out in sequence.

sections.title: When one card is not enough
items: A second H100 buys capacity and lanes, not a smarter model: on the October 2026 index nothing from a non-Chinese lab that fits two H100s beats Gemma 4 31B. Run Gemma tensor-parallel across two cards for throughput, or add a second lane.
The real steps up are GPU-count steps: four cards (Inkling-Small at NVFP4, 171 GB), then eight (Mistral Large 4, or the frontier class below).
Managed GPU lanes sell 1, 2, 4 or 8 GPUs per instance. NVLink and SXM are rarely documented on them, so do not plan on them.

recipes.title: GLM-5.2 at FP8: eight B200s in the cloud, eight 96 GB cards in a 4U server at home
recipes.summary: A 744B mixture-of-experts with about 40B parameters active per token is capacity-bound, not compute-bound: hold the weights, stream the experts. The FP8 checkpoint is 744 GB, so FP8 means eight cards wherever it runs. The cloud node is tuned for speed; the local server is FP8 parity you own; a two-card workstation runs a 4-bit copy.

specs.v: 8 × B200 180 GB, 1,536 GB · $47 an hour, about $34,300 a month warm at list · Azure `ND GB200 v6` · AWS `p6` · Google Cloud `A4` · reference lane `nf-gpu-b200-180-8g` · FP8 weights and KV with room for the 1M window

8 × H200 141 GB, 1,128 GB · $25 an hour, about $18,300 a month warm · spot about $14.60 an hour · Azure `ND H200 v5` · AWS `p5e` · Google Cloud `A3 Ultra` · reference lane `nf-gpu-h200-141-8g` · context up to 256K

8 vCPU · 32 GB · about $288 a month · the Portal, one OpenClaw gateway per user and the failover router · Azure `D8s v5` · AWS `m6i.2xlarge` · Google Cloud `n2-standard-8` · reference lane `nf-compute-800-32`
Decode per stream follows memory bandwidth: B200 HBM3e about 8 TB/s, H200 4.8 TB/s, a 96 GB Blackwell card 1.8 TB/s. FP8 KV cache and expert parallelism (`--enable-moe-ep`) on all three
ASUS ESC8000A-E13 4U · 2 × EPYC 9355 · 768 GB DDR5-5600 RDIMM · 8 × RTX PRO 6000 Max-Q = 768 GB VRAM · the 744 GB checkpoint in VRAM, ~24 GB left for KV
2 × RTX PRO 6000 Max-Q (192 GB) · Threadripper PRO 7975WX · 512 GB DDR5-5600 across eight channels · 10–18 tokens per second decode
`zai-org/GLM-5.2` on Hugging Face, MIT · a 1.5 TB or larger volume, fetched at boot · SGLang or vLLM at FP8, llama.cpp or KTransformers for the 4-bit box

recipes.launch:
# cloud node (B200 or H200) and the eight-card server: the same line
python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path zai-org/GLM-5.2 --tp 8 --quantization fp8 --enable-moe-ep --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e5m2 --context-length 262144 --port 8000

# two-card workstation, 4-bit GGUF, experts in system memory
./llama-server -m GLM-5.2-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf -ngl 99 -t 32 -c 131072 --flash-attn --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --port 8000

sections.title: Why this shape
items: Only about 40B parameters are active per token, so decode is bound by how fast the experts can be read, not by compute. That is why the B200 node is the fast one and why the eight-card server, at GDDR7 speed, is parity rather than speed.
Scale is coarse: each replica is another eight-GPU node. Schedule the frontier node for live load and keep a smaller class as the floor.
The front door does not change: OpenClaw points at one endpoint, and a router adds failover to the economy node, a quantized fallback or a second region.

sections.title: What we would not do
items: Try FP8 on six cards: 576 GB cannot hold a 744 GB checkpoint. Eight is the minimum, and eight leaves about 24 GB for KV, which is fine for a few long conversations and not for a busy tenant.
Put a single 31B tenant on an eight-GPU-only cloud: the wrong unit economics. The eight-card node is the right shape for the frontier class only.
Buy the passive Server Edition from a marketplace seller at $30,000 a card. The Max-Q blower was made for dense boxes and Newegg sells it directly.

sections.title: The local boxes
items: The FP8 server is the chosen local build on the references tab: every part at Newegg's price, about 3.2 kW on a dedicated 240 V circuit, the same launch line as the cloud node.
The two-card workstation is the cheaper path: a 4-bit copy at 10–18 tokens per second, with the experts streaming from 512 GB of system memory.
